EMBRYOLOGY__Applied / Clinical:
Why this matters: when development goes wrong you get congenital anomalies — and each one traces back to a specific step. This subtab ties embryology to the clinic: teratogens & critical periods, neural-tube defects, congenital heart disease and the classic GI, renal & facial malformations you’ll be examined on and will meet in paediatrics.
Teratogens & Critical Periods
Timing
  • Weeks 1–2 — “all-or-none” (the embryo dies or fully recovers)
  • Weeks 3–8 (embryonic/organogenesis) — the period of greatest teratogenic sensitivity (major structural defects)
  • Weeks 9+ (fetal) — growth & functional maturation (milder/functional defects)
Key teratogens
  • Alcohol → fetal alcohol syndrome (the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability)
  • Thalidomide → limb defects (phocomelia); warfarin, ACE inhibitors, retinoids, valproate/phenytoin
  • Rubella (TORCH) → cataracts, deafness, PDA; folate deficiency → neural-tube defects
Neural Tube & CNS Defects
Failed neural tube closure (by week 4): anencephaly (cranial end) & spina bifida (caudal end).
Spina bifida — occulta (arch only), meningocele (meninges), myelomeningocele (cord + meninges → deficit).
Prevention & screening — peri-conceptional folic acid; a raised maternal AFP (open defects).
Chiari II & hydrocephalus accompany myelomeningocele.
Congenital Heart Disease
Acyanotic (L→R shunt or obstructive)
  • VSD (commonest CHD), ASD, PDA
  • The ductus arteriosus is closed by indomethacin (an NSAID) & kept open by prostaglandin E (a lifeline in duct-dependent lesions)
  • Coarctation of the aorta (obstructive, acyanotic) — radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, rib notching; critical neonatal coarctation is duct-dependent
Cyanotic (R→L shunt)
  • Tetralogy of Fallot — VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis & RV hypertrophy (“boot-shaped” heart, “tet spells”)
  • Transposition of the great arteries — needs mixing (PDA/ASD) to survive
Gastrointestinal Anomalies
AnomalyOrigin / clue
Oesophageal atresia + TOFForegut septation defect; polyhydramnios, VACTERL
Duodenal atresiaFailed recanalisation; “double bubble”, Down syndrome
Midgut malrotation / volvulusAbnormal rotation → bilious vomiting, ischaemia
GastroschisisGut herniates right of the umbilicus, NO covering sac; usually isolated
Omphalocele (exomphalos)Gut herniates through the umbilicus, COVERED by a sac; associated anomalies/chromosomal
Meckel’s diverticulumPersistent vitelline duct (rule of 2s)
Hirschsprung’s diseaseFailed neural-crest migration → aganglionic segment
Pyloric stenosisHypertrophy → projectile non-bilious vomiting, an “olive” mass
Gastroschisis vs omphalocele. Gastroschisis = to the right of the cord, no sac, few other anomalies. Omphalocele = at the cord, covered by a sac (peritoneum/amnion), strongly associated with other & chromosomal anomalies.
Genitourinary Anomalies
Horseshoe kidney — fused lower poles caught under the inferior mesenteric artery as it ascends.
Bilateral renal agenesis — oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb/facial deformity).
Hypospadias — the urethral opening is on the ventral penis (failed fusion of the urethral folds).
Cryptorchidism — undescended testis; risk of infertility & malignancy.
Bladder exstrophy — a failure of the anterior abdominal/bladder wall.
Head & Neck / Face & Others
Face & neck
  • Cleft lip — failed fusion of the maxillary & medial nasal prominences
  • Cleft palate — failed fusion of the palatine shelves
  • Branchial (2nd-arch) cyst/fistula & thyroglossal cyst — persistent embryonic remnants
Other high-yield defects
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek — posterolateral, usually left) → bowel in the thorax → pulmonary hypoplasia
  • Twinning — dizygotic (two eggs) vs monozygotic (one egg splits; chorionicity depends on timing; a late split → conjoined twins)
🧠 Mnemonics
Weeks 3–8 = organogenesis = maximum teratogen risk.
Gastroschisis — no Sac, right of cord (“Guts out, no Gift-wrap”); omphalocele = covered.
Duodenal atresia = double bubble + Down.
Prostaglandin keeps the duct Patent; indomethacin closes it.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Organogenesis (weeks 3–8) is the most teratogen-sensitive period; weeks 1–2 = all-or-none.
Fetal alcohol syndrome is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability.
Folic acid prevents neural-tube defects; raised maternal AFP screens for them.
VSD is the commonest CHD; Tetralogy of Fallot is the commonest cyanotic CHD.
PGE keeps the ductus open (duct-dependent lesions); indomethacin closes a PDA.
Duodenal atresia = double bubble, associated with Down syndrome.
Gastroschisis = no sac, right of the cord; omphalocele = sac-covered, more anomalies.
Hirschsprung’s = failed neural-crest migration (aganglionosis).
Renal agenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia).
Bochdalek diaphragmatic hernia → bowel in the chest → pulmonary hypoplasia.
EMBRYOLOGY__General / Early Development:
The first 8 weeks in one glance: fertilisation (week 1) → a hollow blastocyst that implants and becomes a bilaminar disc (week 2) → gastrulation turns it into a trilaminar disc with three germ layers (week 3) → neurulation & folding convert a flat disc into a C-shaped embryo with organ primordia (weeks 4–8). Learn the “1-2-3” rhythm and the germ-layer derivatives — almost every exam question and anomaly hangs off this scaffold.
Week 1 — Fertilisation, Cleavage & the Blastocyst
Fertilisation → morula
  • Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube; sperm penetration triggers the cortical (zona) reaction blocking polyspermy and completes meiosis II of the oocyte
  • Restores the diploid (46) number and determines genetic sex (sperm carries X or Y); the fertilised egg is the zygote
  • Cleavage — a series of mitotic divisions (no growth) producing smaller blastomeres; a solid ball of ~16 cells is the morula (~day 3–4)
Blastocyst (~day 5)
  • Fluid enters to form the blastocyst: a blastocele (cavity), an eccentric inner cell mass / embryoblast (→ embryo) and an outer trophoblast (→ placenta)
  • The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida (~day 5–6), which is prerequisite for implantation
  • All movement/nutrition so far is within the tube/uterus; the conceptus reaches the uterine cavity by ~day 4–5
Clinical link: if the blastocyst implants outside the uterine body — most commonly the ampulla of the tube — the result is an ectopic pregnancy (life-threatening rupture/haemorrhage). Failure to hatch/implant is a cause of early IVF failure.
Week 2 — Implantation & the Bilaminar Disc (“week of twos”)

Almost everything in week 2 comes in pairs — two trophoblast layers, two embryoblast layers, two cavities.

Trophoblast splits in two
  • Cytotrophoblast — inner, mitotically active cellular layer
  • Syncytiotrophoblast — outer multinucleate mass that invades the endometrium and secretes hCG (basis of the pregnancy test; maintains the corpus luteum)
  • Implantation is interstitial (fully embedded) by ~day 10
Embryoblast splits in two
  • Epiblast (columnar, dorsal) and hypoblast (cuboidal, ventral) = the bilaminar disc
  • Two cavities appear: the amniotic cavity (within the epiblast) and the primary yolk sac (lined by hypoblast)
  • Extra-embryonic mesoderm forms and cavitates into the chorionic cavity (extra-embryonic coelom), leaving the connecting stalk (future umbilical cord)
Week 3 — Gastrulation & the Trilaminar Disc (“week of threes”)

Gastrulation is the defining event of week 3: it converts the two-layered disc into a three-layered (trilaminar) disc and establishes the body axes.

The primitive streak
  • A midline groove — the primitive streak — appears in the epiblast, defining the craniocaudal axis, left/right and dorsal/ventral
  • Epiblast cells migrate through the streak (invagination): first replacing hypoblast to become endoderm, then forming the middle mesoderm; cells remaining in the epiblast become ectoderm
  • Thus all three germ layers derive from epiblast
Node, notochord & firsts
  • The primitive node (cranial end of the streak) forms the notochord — the midline axial rod that induces neurulation and becomes the nucleus pulposus
  • Two membranes lack mesoderm and stay bilaminar: the oropharyngeal (future mouth) and cloacal (future anus/urogenital) membranes
  • The cardiovascular system is the first organ system to function (heart beating ~day 22)
Clinical link: persistence of the primitive streak can give a sacrococcygeal teratoma (commonest tumour of the newborn). Abnormal gastrulation is associated with caudal regression / sirenomelia (maternal diabetes) and situs abnormalities.
Germ-Layer Derivatives
Germ layerSubdivisionMajor derivatives
EctodermSurface ectodermEpidermis, hair, nails, lens & cornea epithelium, inner ear, enamel, anterior pituitary, mammary/sweat/salivary glands
Neuroectoderm & neural crestNeural tube → CNS, retina, posterior pituitary. Neural crest → PNS & sensory ganglia, autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, Schwann cells, most facial/skull bones, odontoblasts, aorticopulmonary septum
MesodermParaxial (somites)Axial skeleton, skeletal muscle, dermis of back
IntermediateKidneys, gonads & genital ducts
Lateral plateCardiovascular system, blood, spleen, serous membranes (pleura/peritoneum/pericardium), limb & body-wall connective tissue, adrenal cortex
Endoderm—Epithelial lining of the GI & respiratory tracts, liver, pancreas, biliary tree, thyroid/parathyroid, thymus, bladder & urethra, tympanic cavity/auditory tube
Memory hook: “Ectoderm = attractoderm” (what attracts a partner — skin & nervous system, the outside & the brain). Endoderm = the inner tubes & their glands. Mesoderm = the meat in between (muscle, bone, blood, kidney, gonad, heart).
Neurulation & the Neural Crest (weeks 3–4)
The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate.
The plate folds into neural folds that meet to form the neural tube (→ brain & spinal cord) — neurulation.
Neural crest cells delaminate from the fold tips and migrate widely — the “fourth germ layer”.
The cranial neuropore closes ~day 25, the caudal ~day 28; failure → anencephaly / spina bifida.
Folding & the End of the Embryonic Period (weeks 4–8)
Folding (week 4)
  • Cephalocaudal folding (head/tail) and lateral folding convert the flat trilaminar disc into a C-shaped, cylindrical embryo
  • Folding pulls the endoderm into a primitive gut tube (foregut–midgut–hindgut) and brings the connecting stalk & yolk sac together at the future umbilicus
  • The heart and oropharyngeal membrane are carried ventrally into the neck/thorax
Weeks 4–8: organogenesis
  • All major organ systems form from the germ layers — this is the embryonic period and the time of greatest teratogen sensitivity
  • Pharyngeal (branchial) arches, limb buds, face and body form; by the end of week 8 the embryo is recognisably human
  • From week 9 the fetal period begins — growth and functional maturation rather than new organ formation
Placenta & Fetal Membranes (essentials)
The placenta = fetal chorion frondosum (villous trophoblast) + maternal decidua basalis; site of gas/nutrient/waste exchange.
Chorionic villi: primary (cytotrophoblast) → secondary (+ mesoderm) → tertiary (+ fetal vessels) enable exchange.
The amnion enlarges to surround the fetus (amniotic fluid); the umbilical cord carries 2 arteries + 1 vein.
hCG from syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production (~week 8–10).
Mnemonics
“1-2-3” — week 1 = fertilisation/blastocyst; week 2 = bilaminar (twos); week 3 = trilaminar (threes, gastrulation).
Trophoblast layers — “Cyto is the cellular inner layer; Syncytio secretes hCG and invades.”
All three germ layers come from epiblast — the hypoblast contributes to the yolk-sac lining, not the embryo proper.
Notochord → nucleus pulposus; it induces the neural plate then largely disappears.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube; the commonest ectopic site is also the ampulla.
Blastocyst = embryoblast (→ embryo) + trophoblast (→ placenta) + blastocele; it must hatch from the zona pellucida to implant.
Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG (pregnancy test) and invades the endometrium.
Gastrulation (week 3) forms the three germ layers from epiblast via the primitive streak.
The notochord induces neurulation and becomes the nucleus pulposus.
Neural crest = the “fourth germ layer”: PNS, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, aorticopulmonary septum, most facial bones.
Organogenesis (weeks 3–8) is the most teratogen-sensitive period; the fetal period begins at week 9.
The cardiovascular system is the first organ system to function (~day 22).
